Welcome

A city unlike anywhere else in the Americas

Mérida has quietly become one of the most sought-after destinations in the world for retirees, expats, and real estate investors. The capital of Yucatán blends colonial grandeur, modern infrastructure, genuine safety, and a cost of living that can be half — or less — of what you're used to back home.

This guide is written specifically for non-Mexicans navigating the Mérida property market. Whether you want to retire here, spend part of the year enjoying the culture, or generate passive rental income, we cover everything: legalities, neighborhoods, budgets, the buying process, and the questions most people don't think to ask until it's too late.

Legal Framework

How Foreigners Own Property in Mérida

Here's the one thing every foreign buyer needs to understand upfront: Mérida sits approximately 30km from the Gulf of Mexico coast — well within Mexico's constitutionally defined "restricted zone" (50km from any coastline). This means that unlike some inland cities, all foreigners purchasing property in Mérida and across the Yucatán region must do so through a fideicomiso — a bank trust. This is not a barrier. It's standard practice, extremely well-established, and provides you with full ownership rights.

A fideicomiso is simply the legal vehicle through which your property rights are held. You are the beneficiary of the trust, with all the same rights as any owner: to use, rent, renovate, sell, or leave the property to your heirs.

What is a fideicomiso?

A bank trust authorized by the Mexican government. A Mexican bank (the trustee) holds legal title on your behalf. You are named beneficiary — with complete rights to use, rent, renovate, sell, and pass on the property.

What does it cost?

Setup costs run approximately $1,000–$1,500 USD (paid at closing). Annual bank trust fees are typically $500–$800 USD per year, paid to the Mexican bank. It's a predictable, modest carrying cost.

How long does it last?

Fideicomisos are granted for 50 years and are renewable indefinitely. There is no concern about the trust "expiring" — renewals are routine and inexpensive.

Can I sell through a fideicomiso?

Absolutely. Selling a property held in a fideicomiso is exactly the same process as any other sale in Mexico. The buyer simply takes over as beneficiary, or a new trust is created.

Bottom line: Hundreds of thousands of foreign nationals own property through fideicomisos in Mexico. Your agent, notario, and attorney will handle the entire process. It adds minor cost but zero complication to your lifestyle or ownership rights.

Visas & Residency

Do You Need to Live Here to Own?

No — and this surprises many buyers. You can own property in Mérida on a tourist visa and visit as often as you like. Residency is a separate decision, driven by how much time you want to spend here and the lifestyle benefits that come with it.

Mexico's residency system is straightforward and well-worn by thousands of expats. Owning property can support your application but doesn't automatically grant residency — income or asset thresholds are what the government primarily looks at.

TN

Tourist Visa (FMM): Up to 180 days per visit. No restrictions on owning property. Many part-time residents use this indefinitely by simply crossing the border periodically.

TR

Temporal Residency: 1–4 years, renewable. Required income or asset threshold (approx. $2,600 USD/month or $43,000 USD in savings). Allows you to work, open bank accounts easily, and stay year-round.

PR

Permanente Residency: Available after 4 years of Temporal, or immediately if you meet higher income thresholds. No renewal required. Full rights minus voting.

!

Property & residency: Owning real estate in Mexico can be included in a residency application as an asset, but the process is handled separately. We can connect you with a trusted immigration attorney.

The Process

Buying Step by Step

The Mexican property purchase process is well-organized and foreigner-friendly. Here's what to expect from first interest to holding your keys.

01

Define your goals & budget

Are you buying to live full-time, part-time, or as a pure investment? Your answer shapes everything: neighborhood, property type, required condition, and whether rental income matters. Be honest about renovation capacity too — many Centro properties are sold in need of work.

02

Engage a buyer's agent

Mexico has no formal MLS. Listings are fragmented across agents, developers, and private sellers. A good buyer's agent saves weeks of searching, knows realistic pricing, speaks Spanish, and has relationships with trusted attorneys and notarios. Ask specifically about their experience with foreign buyers.

03

Property search & visits

Plan at least 1–2 weeks for a dedicated visit. Photos rarely capture a property's true condition or the feel of a neighborhood. Visit at different times of day. Talk to neighbors. Check the roof, drainage, and electrical — common issues in older Mérida homes.

04

Offer & promissory contract

When you've found your property, a formal offer is presented. If accepted, a promissory contract (Contrato de Promesa) is signed and a deposit of typically 10% is paid to secure the property during due diligence. Review this contract with your attorney before signing.

05

Due diligence

Your notario and attorney verify: clean title with no liens; proper registration in the Public Registry; no outstanding property taxes; land use compliance; and fideicomiso permit approval from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Allow 4–8 weeks.

06

Closing at the notaría

Both parties (or legal representatives) appear before the notario público. Balance is paid via wire transfer, the escritura is signed, the fideicomiso trust is formalized, and the transfer is recorded with the Public Registry and SAT.

Closing Costs to Budget

Plan for approximately 6–10% of purchase price in total closing costs:

Acquisition Tax (ISAI)Approx. 2% of purchase price — paid by buyer

For Investors

The Mérida Investment Case

Mérida's rental market is strong and growing on two fronts: short-term vacation rentals driven by booming tourism, and long-term expat and professional rentals. Both markets are underserved relative to demand.

6–12%

Short-Term Rental Yield

Gross annual yield on well-located Centro properties with strong Airbnb and Vrbo occupancy rates.

4–7%

Long-Term Rental Yield

More stable and lower management intensity. Expat and professional tenant demand is consistent and growing.

5–10%

Annual Appreciation

Consistent property value growth in desirable neighborhoods over the past decade, driven by international demand.

Tax note: As a foreign owner earning rental income in Mexico, you are subject to Mexican income tax (ISR). Mexico and the US/Canada have tax treaties that prevent double taxation, but you must file in both countries. Engage a Mexican contador and an international tax advisor from the start.

Before You Buy

Things Most People Learn Too Late

Buying in Mérida is genuinely achievable — thousands of expats and investors have done it successfully. These are the things that separate a smooth purchase from an expensive lesson.

Build your team early. You'll need a buyer's agent experienced with foreign clients, a bilingual Mexican attorney, a licensed home inspector, a Mexican accountant, and a Mexican bank account.

!

Visit before you commit. Spend real time in Mérida before buying. The summer heat (April–June), neighbourhood noise levels, and logistics of daily life can only be understood by being there.

!

Get a proper inspection. Drainage, roof, electrical, and structural issues are common in older properties. A few hundred dollars now can save tens of thousands later.

!

Budget for renovation realistically. Labor is affordable but materials are not cheap, and project timelines in Mexico often extend. Add 20–30% buffer to any renovation estimate.

!

Don't skip the attorney. Saving $2,000 on legal fees is not worth discovering a title problem after closing. Due diligence is non-negotiable.

!

Annual costs are low. Property tax (predial) is typically just $100–$400 USD/year for residential property. Factor in insurance, maintenance, and fideicomiso fees.

Key Terms

Words You'll Hear

A quick reference for the Spanish and legal terms that come up in every Mérida property transaction.

Fideicomiso

Bank trust through which foreigners hold property in Mexico's restricted zone. Provides full ownership rights via a Mexican bank as trustee.

Notario Público

A government-licensed legal professional who verifies and records property transactions. Represents the deal — not you personally. Engage your own attorney separately.

Escritura

The official title deed. Signed at closing before the notario and registered with the Public Registry — your proof of ownership.

Promesa de Compraventa

The promissory contract signed when an offer is accepted. Secures the property with a deposit (typically 10%) while due diligence is completed.

Predial

Annual property tax, paid to the municipality. Remarkably low in Mexico — typically $100–$400 USD/year for residential property.

ISAI

Acquisition tax paid by the buyer at closing. Approximately 2% of the purchase price — the main tax cost in a Mexican property transaction.

SAT

Mexico's tax authority (Servicio de Administración Tributaria). Transactions are registered here; rental income is reported here. Your contador handles this.

Contador Público

A Mexican accountant. Essential if you earn rental income — they handle your SAT filings, ISR (income tax), and keep you compliant as a foreign owner.
